newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures end higher, except yen.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures end higher, except yen.

text.p: IMM currency futures closed higher, except for yen which expanded losses as traders unwound long yen/short mark positions, floor sources said.
They said the mark/yen cash cross activity was reflected in the futures pits where dealers gently bid for marks, as yen continued to grind lower.
The profit-taking in mark/yen was spurred after the U.S. April international trade data alleviated market concerns ahead of the Group of Seven (G7) meeting this weekend.
"A lot of long yen and short mark positions were set ahead of Japanese and U.S. trade numbers," one trader said.
He said long yen/short mark positions were taken on ideas the U.S. would continue to pressure Japan to stimulate their economy and avoid a sustained increase in its trade surplus.
Traders and analysts said an appreciation in the yen would be one of the ways Japan could avoid continued gains in their trade surplus.
On Thursday, President Clinton said on Japan's Fuji television network that exchange rates should not be used as a way to correct trade imbalances.

Clinton said he was concerned about Japan's large trade surplus, but said he understood that Japan was taking steps to boost domestic economic demand. Late Wednesday, U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin said it was "very important" that Japan achieve domestic demand-led growth.
However, traders and dealers ignored the comments due to the U.S. April trade deficit, which rose less than expected to $8.36 billion, from March's downwardly revised deficit of $7.76 billion.
Traders, on average, had been looking for the U.S. trade gap to rise to $10 billion in April.
"With those kind of trade numbers, there isn't that type of pressure going into G7," Andy Busch, senior foreign exchange trader at the Bank of Montreal, said.
White House economic advisor Janet Yellen said the trade figures confirmed robust growth in U.S. exports.
The market also showed little reaction to French prime minister Lionel Jospin's comments during his maiden policy statement.
September marks rose above Wednesday's high of $0.5837, but held below trendline resistance at $0.5850. September set a session high at $0.5845 late in the day.
However, the contract found little momentum any time it rose above $0.5841, as institutional bids kept the dollar/mark supported around 1.7225 spot, another trader said.
Meanwhile September Swiss francs rallied through their 50-day moving average at $0.7025, while September sterling rose above their three-week high to $1.6466.

At the end of pit trade, September yen lost $0.000032 at $0.008885, marks were up $0.0039 at $0.5843, Swiss francs rose $0.0054 at $0.7035, sterling rose $0.0100 at $1.6450, Canadian dollars rose $0.0022 at $0.7252, Australian dollars rose $0.0007 at $0.7511 and Mexican pesos were $0.000750 lower at $0.121125.
